title: Introduction to TensorFlow Serving 🍽️
description: Learn how TF Serving delivers models via high‑performance gRPC/REST APIs.

slides.title: From Training to Production 🏭
slides.content:
# The Model Serving Problem

Once you have a trained model, how do you make it available to applications?
- Embed it directly (Python only, not scalable).
- Write a custom web server (Flask, FastAPI) with TensorFlow backend.
- Use a specialised system: **TensorFlow Serving**.

TF Serving is a high‑performance, production‑ready system for serving machine learning models.

slides.title: What is TensorFlow Serving? ⚙️
slides.content:
# Key Features

- **C++ server** (high throughput, low latency).
- **gRPC and REST** endpoints.
- **Model versioning**: serve multiple versions simultaneously; canary deployments.
- **Automatic batching** of requests.
- **Hot reloading**: add new models without downtime.

> Analogy: A professional restaurant kitchen (TF Serving) vs a home cook (Flask + TF). Both serve food, but one is designed for thousands of orders per second.

slides.title: Serving Architecture (Conceptual)
slides.content: Your app sends a request to the server, which loads the SavedModel and returns predictions.

quizData.question: Which communication protocols does TensorFlow Serving support?
quizData.explanation: TF Serving provides both gRPC and RESTful HTTP endpoints.

slides.title: Model Versioning 📚
slides.content:
# Serve Multiple Versions Smoothly

By default, TF Serving serves the highest version number. You can specify a specific version in the request URL.

Folder structure:
```
models/
  my_model/
    1/
      saved_model.pb
      variables/
    2/
      saved_model.pb
      variables/
```

This allows A/B testing and gradual rollbacks.

slides.title: Serving is Not Just for Production 💡
slides.content: You can run TF Serving locally inside Docker to test your SavedModel exactly as it will run in production, catching issues early.
